/Issued 432 AM MST Thu Nov 26 2026/ 

 - Meteorological Overview:

A zonal flow aloft will increase in magnitude today as a fast moving 
shortwave and attendant Pacific moisture moves over the region. A 
robust pressure gradient already developing this morning will 
combine with the strengthening cross barrier flow to result in 
strong winds, initially along the immediate eastern slopes of the 
Rocky Mountain Front, before mountain wave activity shifts further 
east onto the adjacent plains later this morning or early
afternoon. Gusts in excess of 70 mph will be common where the 
mountain wave sets up, which will initially be along the Rocky 
Mountain Front. A second round of strong winds looks to develop near
the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountain Front this evening as a 
secondary mountain wave redevelops. It will gradually weaken 
through the night tonight, allowing for wind concerns to decrease 
along the Rocky Mountain Front toward Friday morning. 

Meanwhile further east over the remaining plains most areas look to 
simply be on the gusty side (sub-warning criteria). The timing of
the strongest winds aloft is late afternoon through the evening, 
which does leave a narrow window for stronger winds to be mixed to
the surface toward sunset. The area with the most persistent risk
for strong winds will be in Judith Basin County from mid 
afternoon today through midday Friday. Additional factors such as 
mountain wave activity and a slightly stronger pressure gradient 
will maintain the risk through this timeframe in Judith Basin
County as opposed to elsewhere where the risk is much more narrow
temporally. The wind across the plains slowly decreases Friday 
afternoon and evening. 

The last factor worth mentioning for this initial stronger zonal 
flow will be for a mix of rain and snow near the Continental 
Divide this afternoon into early Friday morning, particularly 
along the Northern Rocky Mountain Front. A pure zonal flow is not 
often productive from a precipitation perspective east of the 
Rocky Mountain Front, so this risk for mainly minor snow looks to 
be right at Marias Pass along US-2. 

Attention then turns to a disturbance diving through a building 
northwest flow across the region late Friday into Saturday ahead of 
upper level ridging off to the west. There is still some north-south 
discrepancies in where exactly the axis of highest QPF develops, but 
most solutions favor somewhere across SW MT as getting the greatest 
amounts. Snow levels begin on the higher side across SW MT Friday
afternoon, mainly in the 5,000ft - 6,000ft range before lowering 
to valley floors into Saturday morning. What makes this situation 
tricky is that the bulk of the precipitation looks to end by mid- 
morning Saturday. This results in a quite narrow window where snow
levels are low enough to result in snow in the valleys and 
precipitation is actually falling. Confidence is highest in SW MT 
passes seeing impactful snowfall from this system, but there 
remains tremendous uncertainty in just how much snow falls (mostly
due to how fast snow levels fall). It should be noted that cold 
temperatures moving in after temperatures end may result in some 
flash freeze potential even after precipitation is done falling 
Saturday morning. The main takeaway for Friday into Saturday 
morning across SW MT is for wintry conditions over the passes, 
with rain eventually transitioning to snow at lower elevations 
into Saturday morning. Those with post-Thanksgiving travel plans 
over SW MT passes Friday night and Saturday morning should be 
aware of the potential for winter driving conditions. 

Aforementioned ridging shifts east across the region Sunday, but 
weakens as it does so. Early Sunday looks dry, but increasingly 
zonal flow aloft with associated Pacific moisture arriving through 
the day will set the stage for an unsettled start to the week. The 
main takeaway for early next week is for temperatures near average 
most days, with areas near the Continental Divide most favored for 
mainly light precipitation. -AM

 - Forecast Confidence & Scenarios:

Wind today and Friday: 

Consideration was given toward including the lower elevations of 
Cascade County in the High Wind Warning for this afternoon and 
evening. The pressure gradient looks to peak early afternoon, though 
the strongest winds just off the surface hold off til around sunset. 
Given this lack of overlap I decided to forego a High Wind Warning. 
That said, forecast soundings do show 50 kt winds around 2,000ft 
off the surface this evening. Should confidence rise in any mountain 
wave activity developing over this timeframe, or if the peak of the 
pressure gradient trends later, a High Wind Warning may become 
necessary.
